cues.caption: Welcome back, champ!
cues.text: Hey champ! Welcome back. Today is a very special day.

cues.caption: Last time: data, and keeping it private
cues.text: Last time, we learned about data. The facts computers remember, like names and scores. And we learned that private data stays private.

cues.caption: Chapter 5 · Capstone: Design Your Dream App
cues.text: Today is chapter five, the final chapter of Computers in Our World. It's your capstone. Design your dream app!

cues.caption: Capstone = your big, final project
cues.text: Capstone. Hmm, what's that? A capstone is the very last stone, placed right on top of a building. So this is your big, final project!

cues.caption: You're the designer! No coding needed
cues.text: Today, you are the app designer. And guess what? No coding needed. Just a clear idea, a pencil, and your imagination.

cues.caption: Meet Kabir, Class 4
cues.text: Meet Kabir. He's in class four, and he's a lovely kid. But he has one big problem.

cues.caption: Kabir keeps forgetting things!
cues.text: Every morning, he packs his bag in a big rush. And every week, he forgets something. His maths book. His drawing book. His water bottle!

cues.caption: "Kabir, where's your maths book?"
cues.text: At school, his teacher asks, Kabir, where's your maths book? And Kabir says, oh no. I forgot it, again.

cues.caption: What app would help Kabir? Think!
cues.text: What if an app could help Kabir? What would you make for him? Think for a moment.

cues.caption: Idea: Bag Buddy! Let's design it.
cues.text: Here's one idea. An app called, Bag Buddy! Let's design it together, step by step. Then you'll design your own.

cues.caption: Four steps to design an app
cues.text: Designing an app takes just four simple steps.

cues.caption: Problem → Plan → 2 screens → 1-minute pitch
cues.text: Step one, find a problem. Step two, write the plan. Step three, draw two screens. And step four, present it in one minute.

cues.caption: Step 1: Help a Class 3–5 child
cues.text: Step one. Find a problem. Your app should help a child in class three, four, or five. Not a rocket, not a factory. Kids just like you!

cues.caption: Homework? Bag? Spellings? Water?
cues.text: So think. What's hard, or boring, for kids your age? Forgetting homework? Packing your bag? Learning spellings? Forgetting to drink water?

cues.caption: Give it a fun name: Bag Buddy, Spell Star
cues.text: Pick one, and give your app a fun name. Like Bag Buddy, or Spell Star!

cues.caption: Step 2: Who? What goes in? What comes out?
cues.text: Step two. Write the plan. A good plan answers three questions. Who uses it? What goes in? And what comes out?

cues.caption: User: the person who uses the app
cues.text: The person who uses your app is called the user. For Bag Buddy, the user is class four kids who forget their books.

cues.caption: Tiffin Timer: who is the user?
cues.text: Quick one! An app called Tiffin Timer reminds kids to eat their lunch at school. Who's the user?

cues.caption: The user is a school child!
cues.text: Not the tiffin box, silly! It's a school child.

cues.caption: Input: what the user gives the app
cues.text: Remember input and output from our very first unit? Input is what the user gives the app. For Bag Buddy, the child taps tomorrow's subjects.

cues.caption: Output: what the app shows back
cues.text: And output is what the app shows back. Bag Buddy shows a checklist of books to pack. Maths book, tick. Drawing book, tick!

cues.caption: Child types a word: input or output?
cues.text: Let's practise. In a spelling app, the child types a word. Is that the input, or the output? Think.

cues.caption: Input! The star shown back is the output.
cues.text: It's the input! The child gives the word to the app. And the star the app shows back? That's the output.

cues.caption: Bus Buddy: what's the output?
cues.text: Now, Riya's app is called Bus Buddy. She types her stop name, and the app shows when the school bus will arrive. What's the output?

cues.caption: Output: the bus arrival time!
cues.text: The bus arrival time on the screen! Riya typing her stop is the input. The time shown back is the output.

cues.caption: Step 3: Draw 2 screens
cues.text: Step three. Draw two screens. A screen is one page of your app. Just two. Not ten, not fifty!

cues.caption: Screen 1: input · tap the subjects
cues.text: Screen one is where the user gives the input. For Bag Buddy, that's buttons for each subject. Maths, English, Science, Art.

cues.caption: Screen 2: output · the checklist
cues.text: Screen two is where the app shows the output. A checklist of books, with a happy message. All packed!

cues.caption: Paper and pencil. No coding needed!
cues.text: And you don't need a computer for this. A pencil, some paper, and a few colours are enough. No coding at all!

cues.caption: Add one idea from earlier chapters
cues.text: Now, add one idea from your earlier chapters. Pick any one of these three.

cues.caption: Variable: a box holding a changing number
cues.text: A variable. Remember? A box that holds a number that changes. Like a star score, or a counter for the glasses of water you drink.

cues.caption: Loop: a reminder every evening
cues.text: A loop. Doing something again and again. Like a reminder that pops up every single evening. Pack your bag!

cues.caption: Safety rule: never ask for a home address
cues.text: Or a safety rule. Like, your app never asks for a home address. Private data stays private!

cues.caption: Which app idea is the clearest?
cues.text: Detective time! Which app idea is the clearest? A, a cool app that does stuff. B, an app for everyone that does everything. C, a game, not sure who plays it yet. Or D, Spell Star. For class three kids. Input, a word they type. Output, a star if it's right.

cues.caption: D! Clear user, input, and output
cues.text: D! It says who the user is, what the input is, and what the output is. Clear and simple. That's a great plan.

cues.caption: Step 4: a one-minute pitch
cues.text: Step four. Present your app in about one minute. That short talk is called a pitch.

cues.caption: Name · User · Input · Output · Screens
cues.text: Say the name of your app. Say who it's for. Say the input, and the output. Then show your two screens.

cues.caption: One reason it helps. Then take a bow!
cues.text: End with one reason it helps kids. Then, take a bow! Everyone claps for you.

cues.caption: Your turn: capstone challenge
cues.text: Okay champ, here's your capstone challenge.

cues.caption: Write: name, user, one input, one output
cues.text: Draw or list four things. Your app's name. Who uses it. One input. And one output. Pause the video, and try it on paper.

cues.caption: Spell Star · Class 3 · types a word → a star
cues.text: Here's one example. Spell Star. For class three kids. Input, the child types a spelling word. Output, a star if it's spelt right. How did yours turn out? I bet it's amazing!

cues.caption: Your app helps a Class 3–5 child
cues.text: Let's remember. Your app helps a child in class three to five.

cues.caption: Plan: name · user · input · output
cues.text: Your plan has a name, a user, an input, and an output.

cues.caption: Draw 2 screens · no coding
cues.text: You draw two screens. No coding needed.

cues.caption: 1-minute pitch + one earlier idea
cues.text: And you present in one minute, with one idea from earlier, like a loop, a variable, or a safety rule.

cues.caption: All 4 units: done!
cues.text: And champ, look how far you've come. How computers work. Thinking like a computer. Building with blocks. And computers in our world.

cues.caption: Computer Science track complete!
cues.text: You've finished the whole Computer Science track! I'm so proud of you. You're a real computer scientist now.

cues.caption: Next: Quiz · Tap Finish
cues.text: Tap Finish, and try your final quiz. Then go design that dream app!
